summary: Delivering HTTPS content across several content delivery networks raises credential management issues. This document defines metadata in the CDNI interface to set up HTTPS delegation, where an upstream CDN gives delegated credentials to a downstream CDN.

eli5.summary: When one delivery company hands your parcel to another, the second company needs permission to show your ID. This describes how that permission is passed along safely.

questions: how do cdns delegate https credentials
how do cdns share https credentials
should private keys be sent through cdni metadata
subtitle: How an upstream CDN hands short-lived TLS credentials to a downstream CDN so it can serve HTTPS on its behalf.

tldr.problem: When content is delivered over HTTPS through more than one content delivery network, the downstream CDN needs a way to prove its identity to browsers without holding the upstream CDN's own certificate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two CDNI objects: FCI.DelegatedCredentials, where the downstream CDN says how many credentials it can use, and MI.DelegatedCredentials, which carries the delegated credentials (and optionally encrypted private keys) from the upstream CDN.
tldr.outcome: A downstream CDN can present a delegated credential in the TLS handshake as defined in RFC 9345. The RFC advises against sending private keys through the metadata interface at all.

today: RFC 9677 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Delegating HTTPS Across CDNs
sections.content:
Delivering content over HTTPS through one or more Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) means somebody has to manage credentials. The problem is sharpest when one entity hands HTTPS delivery to another trusted entity.

RFC 9677 specifies the CDNI Metadata interface for setting up that handoff using delegated credentials as defined in RFC 9345. The two parties are the upstream CDN (uCDN), which holds the certificate, and the downstream CDN (dCDN), which serves the content. It builds on the CDNI framework, requirements and metadata documents (RFC 7336, RFC 7337, RFC 8006).
sections.eli5: One company owns the shop's ID, but another company is doing the actual deliveries. This document is about lending the second company a temporary pass so it can say it is working for the first.

sections.title: How a Delegated Credential Is Used
sections.content:
Under RFC 9345, when a uCDN has delegated to a dCDN, the dCDN presents a delegated_credential instead of its own certificate during the TLS handshake with the User Agent. The dCDN therefore also needs the private key matching the public key inside the delegated credential. With it, the dCDN signs the CertificateVerify message, and the User Agent can check that signature.

RFC 9677 does not change any of that. It only defines how the credentials get from the uCDN to the dCDN using CDNI interfaces: the Footprint and Capabilities Advertisement interface (FCI) and the Metadata interface (MI).
sections.eli5: The visitor checks the temporary pass, and the second company proves the pass really is theirs by using a secret only they hold. This document just explains how the pass gets to them.

sections.title: Advertising Capabilities with the FCI
sections.content:
A dCDN should announce what it supports through the FCI defined in RFC 8008. Inside an FCI.Metadata capability it lists MI.DelegatedCredentials among the MI objects it understands.

This RFC also defines a new object, FCI.DelegatedCredentials, with two properties:

  • number-delegated-certs-supported: an integer, mandatory, giving the maximum number of delegated credentials the dCDN supports. It typically, but not necessarily, matches the number of servers the dCDN designates for delegated credentials.
  • PrivateKeyEncryptionKey: an optional string holding the dCDN's public key in JSON Web Key (JWK) format, which the uCDN MUST use to encrypt any private key it sends.

The uCDN may issue fewer than the maximum. The dCDN may use a single credential on many endpoints, or a different one per endpoint if it was given enough. That choice is the dCDN's.

The FCI object does not cover expiry or renewal. The uCDN SHOULD monitor expiry times and SHOULD refresh credentials through the MI in good time. If a dCDN server holds only expired credentials, it MUST refuse any new TLS connection that needs an up-to-date delegated credential.
sections.eli5: The second company tells the first how many passes it can use, and (if it wants) gives a special lock so the first can send secrets safely. If a pass runs out and is not replaced, the second company must turn visitors away.

sections.title: The MI.DelegatedCredentials Object
sections.content:
The MI.DelegatedCredentials object carries an array called delegated-credentials (mandatory). Each entry is a DelegatedCredentialObject with two properties:

  • delegated-credential (mandatory): a Base64-encoded CertificateEntry from RFC 8446 that MUST contain a DelegatedCredential structure, using the extension in the end-entity certificate's entry.
  • private-key (optional): the private key matching the credential's public key, encrypted as a JSON Web Encryption (JWE) object in compact serialization, with the key as the JWE Ciphertext. The JWE content-type field MAY signal the media type of the encrypted key.

If private-key is left out, the dCDN is assumed to have generated the key pair itself and passed the public key to the uCDN by some out-of-band means. If it is included, it MUST be encrypted with the PrivateKeyEncryptionKey from the FCI. The dCDN retrieves the object from the uCDN using the CDNI metadata distribution mechanisms of RFC 8006.
sections.eli5: The package holds a list of passes. Each pass can come with its secret key, but only locked in a box that only the second company can open. Often the second company makes its own key and just sends the matching public half.

sections.title: The Call Flow
sections.content:
The RFC walks through six steps:

  1. The uCDN is provisioned with a certificate. How it got one is out of scope.
  2. The uCDN generates a set of delegated credentials, either in advance as a pool or on demand when the dCDN announces its maximum.
  3. The dCDN uses the FCI to advertise MI.DelegatedCredentials support and the maximum number of credentials.
  4. The dCDN uses the MI to fetch the MI.DelegatedCredentials array.
  5. A client opens a TLS connection to a dCDN endpoint per RFC 9345, using those credentials.
  6. When credentials are about to expire, the uCDN sends new ones through the MI.
sections.eli5: The first company prepares passes, the second says how many it needs and picks them up, visitors use them, and the first company hands over fresh ones before the old ones run out.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has registered two payload types in the CDNI Payload Types registry: MI.DelegatedCredentials (interface MI/FCI) and FCI.DelegatedCredentials (interface FCI). The first distinguishes delegated credentials MI objects. The second advertises the number of delegated credentials needed, along with any associated capability advertisement.
sections.eli5: The two new kinds of message get official names in a public list so everybody uses the same ones.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
A delegated credential is only useful with its private key, so leaking the credential alone is a limited risk. Credentials are short-lived: RFC 9345 sets a default maximum validity of 7 days. Even so, the RFC says it is NOT RECOMMENDED to send private keys through the MI at all.

If keys are sent, they MUST be JWE-encrypted with the dCDN's PrivateKeyEncryptionKey, which MUST be at least as strong as the key it protects. This method does not offer forward secrecy: if the encryption key is later compromised, all the JWEs sent with it are too, though short lifetimes limit the damage. An attacker who could systematically collect credentials and keys could impersonate dCDN nodes, so the CDNI interfaces must be secured as RFC 8006 describes.

The objects contain no personally identifiable information, but leaked credentials and keys would let an attacker decrypt end-user data sent to the service.
sections.eli5: A pass is useless without its secret key, and passes expire quickly. Still, the safest plan is not to mail the secret key at all, because a thief with both could pretend to be the second company.
